## Importing Candy Data

```{r}
candy_file <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fivethirtyeight/data/master/candy-power-ranking/candy-data.csv"

candy <- read.csv(candy_file, row.names=1)
head(candy)
```

## Exploratory Analysis

We can start our exploratory analysis section by creating a histogram of our data.

> Q8. Plot a histogram of winpercent values using both base R and ggplot2.

```{r}
# Using Base R
hist(candy$winpercent)

# Using ggplot
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(candy) +
  aes(x = winpercent) +
  geom_histogram()
```


> Q9. Is the distribution of winpercent values symmetrical?

- Our plot is mostly symmetrical but it's skewed a little bit to the right.

> Q10. Is the center of the distribution above or below 50%?

```{r}
summary(candy$winpercent)
```

-The center of distribution is below 50%.

> Q11. On average is chocolate candy higher or lower ranked than fruit candy?

```{r}
# Average for chocolate candy
mean(candy$winpercent[candy$chocolate == 1])

# Average for fruity candy
mean(candy$winpercent[candy$fruity == 1])
```


Chocolate candy raned higher than fruit candy.

> Q12. Is this difference statistically significant?

```{r}
chocolate <- candy$winpercent[candy$chocolate == 1]

fruity <- candy$winpercent[candy$fruity == 1]

t.test(chocolate, fruity)
```
Yes our difference is statistically significant because our p value of 2.871e-08 is much smaller than the cutoff of 0.05.

## Overall Candy Ranking

In this section we can sort our data by using different functions.

> Q13. What are the five least liked candy types in this set?

```{r}
head(candy[order(candy$winpercent), ], 5)
```


> Q14. What are the top 5 all time favorite candy types out of this set?

```{r}
head(candy[order(candy$winpercent, decreasing = TRUE), ], 5)
```

> Q15. Make a first barplot of candy ranking based on winpercent values.

```{r}
ggplot(candy) +
  aes(x = winpercent, y = rownames(candy)) +
  geom_col()
```

> Q16. This is quite ugly, use the reorder() function to get the bars sorted by winpercent?

```{r}
ggplot(candy) +
  aes(x = winpercent,
      y = reorder(rownames(candy), winpercent)) +
  geom_col()
```



```{r}
my_cols=rep("black", nrow(candy))
my_cols[as.logical(candy$chocolate)] = "chocolate"
my_cols[as.logical(candy$bar)] = "brown"
my_cols[as.logical(candy$fruity)] = "red"
```

Now Lets try to plot our above arguments:

```{r}
ggplot(candy) + 
  aes(winpercent, reorder(rownames(candy),winpercent)) +
  geom_col(fill=my_cols) +
  ylab("")
```

> Q17. What is the worst ranked chocolate candy?

- The worst ranked chocolate candy is sixlets

> Q18. What is the best ranked fruity candy?

- The best ranked fruity candy is starburst.


## Taking a look at pricepercent

Now we will look at the different types of candy and their prices.

```{r}
library(ggrepel)

# How about a plot of win vs price
ggplot(candy) +
  aes(winpercent, pricepercent, label=rownames(candy)) +
  geom_point(col=my_cols) +
  geom_text_repel(col=my_cols, size=3.3, max.overlaps=5)
```


> Q19. Which candy type is the highest ranked in terms of winpercent for the least money - i.e. offers the most bang for your buck?

```{r}
ord <- order(candy$winpercent, decreasing = TRUE)
head(candy[ord, c("winpercent", "pricepercent")], n=10)
```

- Reese's miniatures can fit into the category of highest ranked in terms of winpercent and the least money based on our table above. This because Reese's miniatures had relatively one of the highest winpercent and the lowest pricepercent.


> Q20. What are the top 5 most expensive candy types in the dataset and of these which is the least popular?

```{r}
ord <- order(candy$pricepercent, decreasing = TRUE)
head( candy[ord,c(11,12)], n=5 )
```
- Based on our table above we see that the most expensive candy types are Nik L Nip, Nestle Smarties, Ring pop, Hershey's Krackel and Hershey's Milk Chocolate. And out of those 5 categories Nik L Nip is the least popular. 


## Exploring the correlation structure

In this section we can explore the corrleations between our variables and pairs.

```{r}
library(corrplot)
cij <- cor(candy)
corrplot(cij)
```




> Q22. Examining this plot what two variables are anti-correlated (i.e. have minus values)?

The two varibles that are anticorrelated are fruity and chocolate, we can see this from the plot since they both have red circles.


> Q23. Use your corrplot result to make a prediction: which variables do you expect will have the largest contributions (i.e. loadings) to PC1 (i.e., drive the most separation between candies along the first principal component)?

I think the most varibles to have a large contribution on PC1 are bar, chocolate and fruity. This becuase based on the grpah above they are showing a lot of corrlelation with other varible son our plot.


## Principal Component Analysis

Now we will run our PCA using the `prcomp` function.

```{r}
pca <- prcomp(candy, scale = TRUE)
summary(pca)
```
We can plot our PC1 and PC2 results.

```{r}
plot(pca$x[,1:2])
```


```{r}

plot(pca$x[,1:2], col=my_cols, pch=16)


```

Another way we can do our plots is using `ggplot`
```{r}
my_data <- cbind(candy, pca$x[,1:3])

# Create the plot
p <- ggplot(my_data) +
  aes(x=PC1, y=PC2,
      size=winpercent/100,
      text=rownames(my_data),
      label=rownames(my_data)) +
  geom_point(col=my_cols)

p
```

We can also use the package `ggrepel` to actually name the different candies on our plots.

```{r}
library(ggrepel)

p + geom_text_repel(size=3.3, col=my_cols, max.overlaps = 7)  + 
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(title="Halloween Candy PCA Space",
       subtitle="Colored by type: chocolate bar (dark brown), chocolate other (light brown), fruity (red), other (black)",
       caption="Data from 538")
```

We can also create interactive and overlapping plots like the one below.

```{r}
library(plotly)

ggplotly(p)
```



```{r}
ggplot(pca$rotation) +
  aes(PC1, reorder(rownames(pca$rotation), PC1)) +
  geom_col()
```


> Q24. Complete the code to generate the loadings plot above. What original variables are picked up strongly by PC1 in the positive direction? Do these make sense to you? Where did you see this relationship highlighted previously?

- The variables that are picked by PC1 strongly in the positive direction is fruity, pluribus and hard. This trend makes sense to me because a lot of the time fruity candies are hard and also contain multiple pieces which is our pluribus variable. We can also see this relationship highloghted in our previous correlation plot.

## Summary

> Q25. Based on your exploratory analysis, correlation findings, and PCA results, what combination of characteristics appears to make a “winning” candy? How do these different analyses (visualization, correlation, PCA) support or complement each other in reaching this conclusion?

- Based on all of our previous analysises the characteristics of a winning candy point to having chocolate or peanut butter and having a bar shape. This is also supported by looking the most liked candies in our data, like twix and snickers. We can also looking at our correlation plots and see that bar,chocolate and winpercent are positively correlated.
